stem:
Mutapa Packaging Ltd is a fictional company in Harare that makes cartons. In 2025 it borrowed US\$89,000 to open a second factory and raised its prices on some lines. The managing director says, "2025 was a success: revenue is up by 18.3%." A bank is now considering a further loan. Summarised figures for the two years are given below (the company's ratios for 2024 are shown after the table).

| US\$ | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 652,400 | 771,800 |
| Cost of sales | 407,300 | 502,500 |
| Expenses | 147,900 | 176,900 |
| Finance costs | 7,600 | 15,700 |
| Tax | 21,100 | 17,400 |
| Dividends | 25,300 | 29,600 |
| Issued shares | 190,000 | 190,000 |
| Reserves | 143,500 | 178,200 |
| Non-current liabilities | 58,000 | 147,000 |
| Current assets | 164,200 | 192,600 |
| of which inventories | 71,600 | 110,300 |
| Current liabilities | 81,900 | 128,400 |
| Trade receivables | 53,300 | 86,500 |
| Credit sales | 574,000 | 703,000 |

| Ratio for 2024 | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Gross profit margin | 37.6% |
| Operating profit margin | 14.9% |
| ROCE | 24.8% |
| Acid test ratio | 1.13 : 1 |
| Gearing | 14.8% |
| Trade receivables days | 34 days |
| Dividend cover | 2.71 times |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Using the data for 2025, calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the gross profit;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the profit from operations;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the profit for the year;

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: the capital employed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the following ratios for 2025 (percentages and days to one decimal place, other ratios to two decimal places):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: ROCE (profit from operations ÷ capital employed × 100);

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the acid test ratio, as x : 1;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the gearing ratio (non-current liabilities ÷ capital employed × 100);

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: the trade receivables (debtor) days, to one decimal place;

parts.label: (v)
parts.stem: the dividend cover (profit for the year ÷ dividends), in times to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Analyse the change in profitability between 2024 and 2025, using the gross profit margin, the operating profit margin and ROCE.

points.description: Gross profit margin fell from 37.6% to 34.9%, so cost of sales rose faster than revenue
Operating profit margin fell from 14.9% to 12.0% as expenses also grew
ROCE fell from 24.8% to 17.9% because profit from operations fell from US\$97,200 to US\$92,400 while capital employed rose from US\$391,500 to US\$515,200
So revenue growth of 18.3% has not produced more profit; the new factory has added capital before profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The gross profit margin fell from 37.6% to 34.9%, so the cost of sales rose faster than revenue, and the operating profit margin fell from 14.9% to 12.0% as expenses also grew. ROCE fell from 24.8% to 17.9% because profit from operations fell from US\$97,200 to US\$92,400 while capital employed rose from US\$391,500 to US\$515,200. Revenue growth of 18.3% has therefore not produced more profit; the new factory has added capital before the profit.

parts.explanation: All three profitability ratios have fallen.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Mutapa Packaging Ltd's 2025 results support the managing director's claim that 2025 was a success, and advise the bank whether to grant a further loan.

points.description: Revenue rose by 18.3%, which supports the claim
But all the profitability ratios fell and profit for the year fell from US\$68,500 to US\$59,300
Liquidity has weakened: the acid test fell from 1.13 : 1 to 0.64 : 1 and inventories rose from US\$71,600 to US\$110,300
Gearing has almost doubled (14.8% to 28.5%) and finance costs have doubled to US\$15,700, so a further loan would add risk
Customers take longer to pay (34 to 45 days), tying up cash; dividend cover has fallen from 2.71 to 2.00, but is still safe
Limitations: one year after an expansion, so profit may recover as the new factory matures; ratios do not show orders or cash flow
Judgement and advice with a condition, for example delay the loan or lend only with security until profit from the new factory rises and liquidity improves

levels.descriptor: Uses figures from profitability, liquidity, gearing and efficiency; weighs the claim against the evidence and the limitations; a justified recommendation with a condition
Uses some figures with some analysis; judgement weakly supported
States ratios or the claim with little analysis

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Revenue rose by 18.3%, which supports the claim, but every profitability ratio fell and profit for the year fell from US\$68,500 to US\$59,300. Liquidity has weakened: the acid test fell from 1.13 : 1 to 0.64 : 1 as inventories rose from US\$71,600 to US\$110,300. Gearing has almost doubled to 28.5% and finance costs have doubled to US\$15,700, so a further loan would add risk. Customers also take longer to pay, about 45 days against 34, which ties up cash, and dividend cover has fallen from 2.71 to 2.00, although it is still safe. The results are for one year after an expansion, so profit may recover as the new factory matures, and ratios do not show orders or cash flow. The claim is not supported by the profit figures. The bank should delay the loan, or lend only against security, until profit from the new factory has risen and liquidity has improved.

parts.explanation: Revenue is up but profit, liquidity and gearing have all worsened; the bank should be cautious.
hints: Use ratios from all four groups.
Remember the limitations and end with advice for the bank.

explanation: Gross profit 269,300; profit from operations 92,400; profit for the year 59,300; capital employed 515,200; ROCE 17.9%, acid test 0.64 : 1, gearing 28.5%, 44.9 days, cover 2.00; the claim is not supported.
hints: Capital employed = shares + reserves + non-current liabilities.
Remember that the acid test removes inventories.
Use both years when you analyse and evaluate.

stem:
Masimba Plastics is a fictional manufacturer of plastic crates in Bulawayo with 46 employees. The directors want to buy a new moulding machine for US\$94,500 so that the company can make a stackable crate, which it would sell for US\$4.65 each against a variable cost of US\$2.95. The extra fixed costs of the new line would be US\$20,060 a year and the company expects to sell 15,500 crates a year. The company can borrow at 13% a year. The machine would last five years. The operations manager says the machine needs skilled operators and that the company's current supplier of plastic granules has been late in delivering twice in the last six months. The marketing manager believes that a rival is about to launch a similar crate at a lower price. Last quarter the company's sales of existing crates were below budget and its spending on materials above budget, and the finance director is worried about a rising overdraft.

| US\$ | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Cost of the machine | 94,500 |
| Net cash inflow, year 1 | 27,400 |
| Net cash inflow, year 2 | 30,900 |
| Net cash inflow, year 3 | 33,600 |
| Net cash inflow, year 4 | 29,300 |
| Net cash inflow, year 5 | 25,700 |
| Budgeted sales last quarter (existing crates) | 121,400 |
| Actual sales last quarter | 114,700 |
| Budgeted materials last quarter | 42,300 |
| Actual materials last quarter | 45,900 |

The discount factors supplied for the project are:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Discount factor at 13% | 0.885 | 0.783 | 0.693 | 0.613 | 0.543 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: For the new crate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the contribution per crate;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: calculate the break-even output in crates a year;

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: calculate the profit at the expected sales of 15,500 crates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: For the machine, using the net cash inflows in the table:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the payback period in years, to two decimal places;
parts.explanation: Cumulative inflows: 27,400; 58,300; 91,900 after year 3. 2,600 is still to be recovered; year 4 brings 29,300, so the fraction = 0.09. Payback = 3.09 years.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: calculate the accounting rate of return (average annual profit ÷ initial investment × 100), to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Total inflows = 146,900. Total profit = 52,400. Average annual profit = 10,480. ARR = 10,480 ÷ 94,500 × 100 = 11.1%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the net present value of the machine at 13%, using the discount factors supplied.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: For last quarter, calculate the size of the variance (direction is not asked for) for:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: sales;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: materials.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Analyse the non-financial factors that the directors should consider before they buy the machine.

points.description: Skilled operators are needed, so training or recruitment will cost money and time
Application: the 46 employees may not have the skills at present, so output may be delayed
The supplier of granules has been late twice, so production could be interrupted
A rival may launch a similar crate at a lower price, so the forecast sales of 15,500 may not be achieved
Overall these risks could lower the cash inflows and the NPV, which depend on forecasts

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The machine needs skilled operators, and the company's 46 employees may not have these skills, so training or recruitment will cost money and delay output. The supplier of granules has been late twice, so production could be interrupted. A rival may launch a similar crate at a lower price, so the forecast sales of 15,500 may not be achieved. These risks could lower the cash inflows and the NPV, which depend on forecasts.

parts.explanation: Skills, suppliers and competition are non-financial risks.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the directors should buy the machine and recommend a course of action.

points.description: NPV is positive (US\$9,144.50 at 13%), so the project earns more than the cost of borrowing
Payback of 3.09 years is fairly long and ARR of 11.1% is below the 13% borrowing cost, so the other methods are less favourable
Break-even of 11,800 crates against 15,500 expected gives a margin of safety of about 24%, but a rival's price cut could remove it
Overdraft is rising and sales and materials are off budget, so the company's finances are under pressure to fund US\$94,500
Judgement and recommendation with a condition, for example buy only if finance is arranged and supply and training risks are tackled

levels.descriptor: Uses several investment results with the finance, supplier, rival and budget information; a justified recommendation with a condition
Uses some results with some analysis; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The NPV of US\$9,144.50 at 13% is positive, so the machine earns more than the cost of borrowing. However, the payback of 3.09 years is fairly long and the ARR of 11.1% is below the 13% cost of borrowing, so the other methods are less favourable. The break-even output of 11,800 crates against 15,500 expected gives a margin of safety of about 24%, but a rival's price cut could remove it. The company's overdraft is rising and its sales and materials are off budget, so funding US\$94,500 would put pressure on its finances. The directors should buy the machine only if they can arrange finance without worsening the overdraft and can deal with the risks from the supplier and from the lack of skills; otherwise they should wait.

parts.explanation: NPV is positive but ARR and payback are weak, and risks and finance pressure are significant.
hints: Compare the three appraisal results, then the risks and the finance.

explanation: Contribution 1.70; break-even 11,800; profit 6,290; payback 3.09 years; ARR 11.1%; NPV 9,144.50; variances 6,700 A and 3,600 A; evaluation with recommendation.
hints: Variances compare the budget with the actual figure.

stem: Essay. Many manufacturing firms in Zimbabwe use budgets to plan and control their activities.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the purposes of budgets and the differences between incremental, flexible and zero-based budgeting. [10 marks]

points.description: A budget is a financial plan in money for a future period
Purpose: to plan and set targets for sales, costs and profit
Purpose: to allocate resources between departments
Purpose: to control spending by making managers responsible
Purpose: to compare actual results with the plan and find variances
Incremental budgeting adjusts last period's figures for expected changes
Development: it is quick but repeats past waste
Flexible budgeting adjusts to the actual level of output
Development: it gives a fair comparison when output differs from the plan
Zero-based budgeting justifies every item from zero, which removes waste but takes time

levels.descriptor: Purposes and all three types clearly described and developed
Purposes and two types described with some development
Names purposes or types with little description

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A budget is a financial plan, in money, for a future period. Firms use budgets to plan and set targets for sales, costs and profit, to allocate resources between departments and to control spending by making managers responsible for their own budgets. Actual results are compared with the plan, and the differences, called variances, show where action is needed. An incremental budget takes last period's figures and adjusts them for expected changes such as inflation; it is quick to prepare but repeats past waste. A flexible budget is adjusted to the actual level of output, so that costs are compared at the same volume; it is fairer when output differs from the plan. A zero-based budget requires every item of expenditure to be justified from zero each period, which removes waste and links spending to need, but it takes a lot of time.

parts.explanation: Purposes and the three types described.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether budgets help a Zimbabwean manufacturing firm to control its costs and improve its performance. [15 marks]

points.description: Budgets set targets for each department, which gives a clear aim
Managers are responsible for spending, which encourages control
Variances show where costs are higher than planned so that action can be taken early
Application: an adverse materials variance could lead to checks on suppliers' prices or waste
Budgets help to allocate scarce resources, such as cash and foreign currency, to the best uses
They coordinate departments so that production, purchasing and sales fit together
Targets can motivate staff, especially if they take part in setting them
Budgets rely on forecasts, which are difficult when prices and exchange rates change quickly
A budget that is too tight may demotivate staff or lead them to cut quality
A budget that is too easy may allow waste
Setting and monitoring budgets takes time and cost, especially zero-based budgeting
Variances need explanation: a flexed budget is needed when output changes
Budgets can be rigid and discourage managers from responding to opportunities
Control also depends on action after the variance is found, not on the budget alone
Judgement: budgets are useful but only if realistic, flexed, reviewed regularly and combined with action, with a reasoned conclusion

levels.descriptor: Balanced argument on benefits and drawbacks applied to a manufacturing firm in changing conditions; a justified, qualified judgement
Benefits and some drawbacks explained with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Budgets can help a manufacturing firm to control costs. They set targets for each department, make managers responsible for spending and, by comparing actual results with the plan, show variances early. For example, an adverse materials variance could lead the firm to check suppliers' prices or wastage. Budgets also help to allocate scarce resources such as cash and foreign currency to the best uses and to coordinate departments so that production, purchasing and sales fit together. Targets can motivate staff, especially if they take part in setting them. However, budgets rely on forecasts, which are difficult when prices and exchange rates change quickly, so a budget can quickly become unrealistic. A budget that is too tight may demotivate staff or lead to cuts in quality, while one that is too easy allows waste. Setting and monitoring budgets takes time and cost, particularly zero-based budgets, and budgets can be rigid and discourage managers from responding to opportunities. Variances also need to be explained: if output differs from the plan, a flexed budget is needed before managers are blamed. Control depends on action after the variance is found, not on the budget alone. Overall, budgets help a manufacturing firm to control costs and improve performance when they are realistic, flexed to actual output, reviewed regularly and followed by action; in unstable conditions they should be revised often.

parts.explanation: Benefits and drawbacks weighed, ending with a qualified judgement.

explanation: Describe purposes and types of budget; discuss benefits and drawbacks and conclude that budgets work when realistic, flexed and followed by action.
hints: Describe each type of budget in (a).
In (b), weigh the benefits against the drawbacks and give a conclusion with a condition.

stem: Essay. A growing business needs to decide which projects to invest in.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how a business can use the payback period and the accounting rate of return to appraise an investment. [10 marks]

points.description: Investment appraisal helps a business to decide whether a large project is worthwhile
Payback is the time taken for the net cash inflows to repay the initial outlay
Development: it is found by adding the cash flows year by year until the outlay is recovered, and the fraction of a year is converted to months
A shorter payback means that the cash returns sooner and the risk is less
ARR is the average annual profit as a percentage of the investment
Development: average annual profit = (total net cash inflows − outlay) ÷ years, then divided by the investment and multiplied by 100
The ARR is compared with a target rate or the cost of borrowing
Payback focuses on liquidity but ignores cash after the payback date
ARR uses all the cash flows but ignores the timing of the cash
Example from a small business, such as a poultry house or a bakery oven

levels.descriptor: Both methods explained with calculations described and uses and limitations; an example
Both methods explained with some development
Defines the methods with little explanation

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Investment appraisal helps a business to decide whether a large project is worth the outlay. The payback period is the time taken for the net cash inflows to repay the initial outlay. It is found by adding the cash flows year by year until the outlay is recovered, and the fraction of the last year is converted into months. A short payback means that cash returns quickly and the risk is lower. The accounting rate of return (ARR) is the average annual profit as a percentage of the investment. The average annual profit is found by taking the total net cash inflows less the outlay and dividing by the number of years, and this is then divided by the investment and multiplied by 100. The result is compared with a target rate or with the cost of borrowing. For example, a bakery that buys an oven for US\$40,000 can use both: payback shows how quickly the oven pays for itself, while ARR shows the average return over its life. Payback focuses on liquidity but ignores cash after the payback date, while ARR uses all the cash flows but ignores the timing of the cash.

parts.explanation: Payback and ARR explained with uses and limits.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether a small business should rely on net present value rather than payback when it makes an investment decision. [15 marks]

points.description: NPV discounts future cash flows to present values and subtracts the outlay
It allows for the time value of money: money today can earn interest and loses value through inflation
It uses all the cash flows over the whole life of the project
A positive NPV shows that the project earns more than the discount rate
It gives a clear accept or reject rule in dollars
Application: a small business borrowing at a known rate can use that rate as the discount rate
Payback is simple and quick to calculate and understand
It focuses on liquidity, which is important for a small business with limited cash
It suits risky projects or fast-changing markets because early cash is less uncertain
Payback ignores cash flows after the payback date, so profitable projects may be rejected
NPV is more complex and depends on the discount rate chosen, which is an estimate
Both methods depend on forecasts of cash flow that may be inaccurate
Qualitative factors such as risk, finance available and political and economic conditions also matter
Different methods can rank projects differently, so using them together gives a fuller view
Judgement: NPV is better for long-term value, but a small business short of cash should also use payback, with a reasoned conclusion

levels.descriptor: Balanced argument on NPV and payback with application to a small business; recognises forecasts and qualitative factors; a justified, qualified judgement
Explains both methods with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Net present value discounts future cash flows to their value today and subtracts the outlay. It allows for the time value of money, because money today can earn interest and inflation reduces the value of money received later. It uses all the cash flows over the life of the project and gives a clear rule in dollars: a positive NPV shows that the project earns more than the discount rate. A small business that borrows at a known rate can use that rate to discount. Payback, in contrast, is simple, quick and easy to understand. It focuses on liquidity, which matters to a small business with limited cash, and it suits risky projects or fast-changing markets because cash that arrives early is less uncertain. But payback ignores cash after the payback date, so a profitable project with large late inflows may be rejected. NPV is more complex, and the result depends on the discount rate chosen, which is itself an estimate. Both methods depend on forecasts of cash flow that may be inaccurate, and qualitative factors such as risk, the finance available and economic and political conditions also matter. Because the methods can rank projects differently, using them together gives a fuller view. NPV is better for judging long-term value, but a small business that is short of cash should also use payback, so it should not rely on NPV alone.

parts.explanation: NPV and payback weighed, ending with a qualified judgement.

explanation: Explain payback and ARR; discuss NPV against payback and conclude that a small business should use both.
hints: Explain the calculation of each method in (a).
In (b), consider liquidity, the discount rate and forecasts before you conclude.
